summary: Self-funded ERISA plans (UMR, Cigna and UHC administrative-services plans, UHC Shared Services, UMWA Funds for non-Medicare members) must answer: written notice of any denial or reduction within 30 days of receiving a post-service claim (one 15-day extension, only with notice before day 30), 180 days for the claimant to appeal, and an appeal decision within 60 days (one level) or 30 days per level (two levels) (29 CFR 2560.503-1). Every notice must state the specific reason, plan provision, denial code and meaning, the plan's standard, the rule or criterion used, and appeal and external review rights (2560.503-1(g); 29 CFR 2590.715-2719(b)(2)(ii)(E)). The claimant gets the whole claim file and the criteria, including third-party rules, free; medical-judgment appeals need a licensed professional in the field, and the plan must identify its experts. If the plan does not strictly follow any of this, the claimant is deemed to have exhausted, may go to external review (medical judgment, No Surprises Act, rescission; binding; immediate payment on reversal) or to federal court, where the claim is deemed denied without discretion, which takes away the plan's usual deferential review (2719(b)(2)(ii)(F)). The plan sponsor also faces a self-reported excise tax of $100 per day per affected person for uncorrected failures of these rules (26 U.S.C. 4980D, 9815). What ERISA does not give: no prompt-pay interest, no state prompt-pay law against self-funded private plans (deemer clause; Kentucky's own definition excludes them), and the $110 per day document penalty runs only against the plan administrator and in favor of the patient. The practice can sue as assignee in the Sixth Circuit for denials and non-payment (Brown v. BCBST, 2016), not for in-network rate or recoupment disputes, which are contract matters. Anti-assignment clauses are the main defense; the Fifth Circuit lets providers argue waiver when the plan never raised the clause, so letters should ask the plan to name any such clause early, and the practice should hold a separate authorized-representative designation. Fully insured commercial plans, Kentucky public-employer and church self-insured plans add state prompt-pay and state external review (state-law area). Non-federal governmental plans follow the same federal rules under 45 CFR 147.136 with CMS penalties up to $188 per day per person. UMWA Funds is a Medicare HCPP for Part B: its Medicare members' claims follow the Medicare Advantage appeal rules (60 days to request, 60-day decision, auto-forward to the CMS IRE). The No Surprises Act matters only when the practice is out-of-network and works at an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ASC (30-day initial payment, open negotiation, IDR). The honest 'teeth' in a letter are: the exact deadline and subsection missed, the deemed-exhaustion consequence with de novo court review, the plan's 10-day duty to explain, the external review that binds the plan, the excise-tax exposure of the sponsor, and the specific next step the practice will actually take.

rules.quote: provide adequate notice in writing to any participant or beneficiary whose claim for benefits under the plan has been denied, setting forth the specific reasons for such denial ... afford a reasonable opportunity to any participant whose claim for benefits has been denied for a full and fair review by the appropriate named fiduciary
rules.applies_to: Every ERISA employee benefit plan: self-funded private-employer plans (UMR, Cigna and UHC administrative-services plans, UHC Shared Services), fully insured employer plans (the insurer decides claims for the plan), and multiemployer plans (UMWA Funds). Not governmental plans or non-electing church plans (29 U.S.C. 1003(b)(1)-(2)).
rules.requires: A written denial stating the specific reasons, and a full and fair review on appeal by a named fiduciary. The detailed rules are in 29 CFR 2560.503-1.
rules.deadline: Set by the regulation (see E02 and E06).
rules.consequence: Enforced through 29 CFR 2560.503-1(l) and 29 CFR 2590.715-2719(b)(2)(ii)(F) (deemed exhaustion) and a civil action under 29 U.S.C. 1132(a)(1)(B).
rules.provider_use: Statutory anchor for every letter to an ERISA plan: the plan must answer in writing with specific reasons. A bare CARC/RARC code without an explanation is not a 'specific reason' under the regulation's content rules (E04).

rules.citation: 29 CFR 2560.503-1(f)(2)(iii)(B) and (f)(4); applied to insurers by 29 CFR 2590.715-2719(b)(2)(i) and to issuers and non-federal governmental plans by 45 CFR 147.136(b)(2)(i)
rules.quote: the plan administrator shall notify the claimant, in accordance with paragraph (g) of this section, of the plan's adverse benefit determination within a reasonable period of time, but not later than 30 days after receipt of the claim. This period may be extended one time by the plan for up to 15 days ... the period of time within which a benefit determination is required to be made shall begin at the time a claim is filed in accordance with the reasonable procedures of a plan, without regard to whether all the information necessary to make a benefit determination accompanies the filing.
rules.applies_to: All group health plans subject to ERISA (self-funded and fully insured; contracted or not when the claim is a claim for benefits, see E11), non-federal governmental plans and health insurance issuers (via 45 CFR 147.136). Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care and VA are governed by their own rules.
rules.requires: Notice of any adverse benefit determination on a post-service claim within 30 days of receipt. One 15-day extension only if the plan, before day 30, sends notice of the circumstances and the date it expects to decide. If the extension is for missing information, the notice must specifically describe the information and the claimant gets at least 45 days to respond; the clock is tolled only from that notice until the response.
rules.deadline: 30 days from receipt of a claim filed under the plan's procedures; plus at most 15 days with a timely extension notice; tolling only for a specific information request.
rules.consequence: No interest or money penalty under ERISA for lateness itself. Missing the deadline is a failure to follow the claims procedure, so the claimant is deemed to have exhausted internal remedies and may go to external review (if eligible) or to court, where the claim is deemed denied without the exercise of discretion (E09).
rules.provider_use: Record the payer's receipt date (277CA or portal acceptance). At day 31 (or day 46 after a timely extension notice) with no determination, send a 'no determination' notice citing (f)(2)(iii)(B) and stating the claim is deemed exhausted. Because a non-payment is itself an adverse benefit determination (E03), silence is a violation, not a pending status.

rules.quote: A denial, reduction, or termination of, or a failure to provide or make payment (in whole or in part) for, a benefit
rules.applies_to: ERISA group health plans and (through 2719 and 45 CFR 147.136) insurers and non-federal governmental plans.
rules.requires: Any full or partial non-payment of a benefit is an adverse benefit determination, which triggers the notice content rules (E04), the 180-day appeal right and the appeal decision deadlines (E06).
rules.deadline: Same as E02 and E06.
rules.consequence: A reduced payment without a compliant notice is a procedural violation (E09).
rules.provider_use: Treat each short-paid or zero-paid line on an out-of-network or benefit-limited claim as an adverse benefit determination and demand a compliant notice. Caution: for in-network lines where the shortfall is a contract-rate question and the practice cannot bill the patient, DOL treats the dispute as contractual, not a benefit claim (E11) - use the provider agreement there.

rules.quote: (i) The specific reason or reasons for the adverse determination; (ii) Reference to the specific plan provisions on which the determination is based; ... The plan and issuer must ensure that the reason or reasons for the adverse benefit determination or final internal adverse benefit determination includes the denial code and its corresponding meaning, as well as a description of the plan's or issuer's standard, if any, that was used in denying the claim.
rules.applies_to: Non-grandfathered group health plans (self-funded and insured) for the 2719 additions; all ERISA group health plans for the 2560.503-1(g) and (j) list.
rules.requires: Every denial or reduction notice must give: the specific reason; the specific plan provision; any information needed to perfect the claim and why; the review procedures and time limits and the right to sue under ERISA 502(a); the internal rule, guideline, protocol or criterion relied on (or a statement it was relied on and is free on request); for medical necessity or experimental denials, the clinical rationale (or a statement it is free on request); claim identification (date of service, provider, claim amount, and that diagnosis and treatment codes and meanings are available on request); the denial code and its meaning; the plan's standard; the internal appeal and external review processes; and consumer-assistance contact information. A final denial must also discuss the decision.
rules.deadline: With each adverse determination (initial and on review).
rules.consequence: A notice missing any element is a failure to 'strictly adhere' to 2719(b)(2), so the internal process is deemed exhausted (E09), unless the plan proves the narrow de minimis exception. The regulation's own Example 1 in 2719(d)(1)(ii) calls a notice that omits the plan's standard 'inadequate'.
rules.provider_use: Have RemitWatch check each EOB/835 response against this list and name the missing elements by subsection in the letter. Typical gaps: no plan provision, no description of the plan's standard, no rule or edit identified for bundling and downcoding, no clinical rationale.

rules.citation: 29 CFR 2560.503-1(h)(2)(iii), (m)(8), (g)(1)(v)(A)-(B), (j)(3); DOL Benefit Claims Procedure FAQs C-17 and D-12
rules.quote: a claimant shall be provided, upon request and free of charge, reasonable access to, and copies of, all documents, records, and other information relevant to the claimant's claim for benefits (2560.503-1(h)(2)(iii)). FAQ C-17: "Yes. It is the view of the department that where a rule, guideline, protocol, or similar criterion serves as a basis for making a benefit determination, either at the initial level or upon review, the rule, guideline, protocol, or criterion must be set forth in the notice of adverse benefit determination or, following disclosure of reliance and availability, provided to the claimant upon request."
rules.applies_to: All ERISA group health plans; insurers and non-federal governmental plans through 2719 and 45 CFR 147.136.
rules.requires: Free copies of everything 'relevant': documents relied on; documents submitted, considered or generated in deciding the claim even if not relied on; documents showing the plan's consistency safeguards; and any statement of policy or guidance on the denied treatment for the diagnosis. Third-party or proprietary criteria must be disclosed (underlying data need not be). DOL also treats internal rules and criteria as instruments under which the plan is operated within ERISA 104(b)(4).
rules.deadline: No day count for the copy request itself; under 2719(b)(2)(ii)(C) new evidence must be given 'as soon as possible and sufficiently in advance' of the appeal decision deadline.
rules.consequence: Not providing the file or the criteria is a procedural violation leading to deemed exhaustion (E09); no deference to a decision based on undisclosed criteria.
rules.provider_use: Send one batched request per payer per denial pattern for: the claim file, the claim-editing rule or edit ID, the clinical policy, the reviewer's identity and credentials, and documents showing consistent application. The regulation does not mention software or AI by name; asking for an automated edit or model rule as a 'similar criterion' is an interpretation, supported by FAQ C-17's inclusion of third-party rules.

rules.quote: Provide claimants at least 180 days following receipt of a notification of an adverse benefit determination within which to appeal the determination ... In the case of a group health plan that provides for one appeal of an adverse benefit determination, such notification shall be provided not later than 60 days after receipt by the plan of the claimant's request for review ... In the case of a group health plan that provides for two appeals ... not later than 30 days after receipt by the plan of the claimant's request for review of the adverse determination.
rules.applies_to: ERISA group health plans; insurers and non-federal governmental plans via 2719 and 45 CFR 147.136 (individual-market issuers: one level only, 45 CFR 147.136(b)(3)(ii)(G)). Multiemployer plans whose board of trustees meets at least quarterly may decide at the next board meeting (or the second if the appeal arrives within 30 days of a meeting; third with special circumstances) under (i)(2)(iii)(B).
rules.requires: Claimant gets at least 180 days from receipt of the adverse determination notice to appeal (the plan may allow more; check the SPD). Post-service appeal decisions: 60 days for a single-level plan, 30 days per level for a two-level plan, counted from receipt of an appeal filed under the plan's procedures even if incomplete.
rules.deadline: Practice: 180 days from receipt of the notice (verify the plan's SPD and any provider-contract limit). Plan: 60 days (one level) or 30 days per level (two levels); multiemployer quarterly-board rule if applicable.
rules.consequence: A late appeal decision means the claimant is deemed to have exhausted and may sue or seek external review; the claim is deemed denied without discretion (E09).
rules.provider_use: Calendar the plan's decision date from your proof of filing. Do not let the plan's provider-manual 'reconsideration' step eat the 180 days: if the plan uses a provider reconsideration step, state in the letter that it is filed as the ERISA appeal on the patient's behalf (with the authorization in E11) or that it is a voluntary level (E07).

rules.quote: do not contain any provision, and are not administered in a way, that requires a claimant to file more than two appeals of an adverse benefit determination prior to bringing a civil action ... The plan waives any right to assert that a claimant has failed to exhaust administrative remedies because the claimant did not elect to submit a benefit dispute to any such voluntary level of appeal ... The plan agrees that any statute of limitations or other defense based on timeliness is tolled during the time that any such voluntary appeal is pending
rules.applies_to: ERISA group health plans (and insurers via 2719).
rules.requires: No more than two mandatory appeal levels; any additional level is voluntary, with exhaustion waived and time limits tolled while it is pending; no fees to file a claim or appeal ((b)(3)); mandatory arbitration only as one of the two appeals and without precluding suit ((c)(4)).
rules.deadline: None of its own.
rules.consequence: A plan that requires a third mandatory level, charges fees, or imposes binding arbitration has unreasonable procedures, so remedies are deemed exhausted.
rules.provider_use: When a payer demands a 'second-level provider dispute' or arbitration before it will pay a benefit claim, cite (c)(2)-(c)(4). For contracted (in-network) rate disputes, the provider agreement's arbitration clause still governs (E11).

rules.quote: the appropriate named fiduciary shall consult with a health care professional who has appropriate training and experience in the field of medicine involved in the medical judgment ... Provide for the identification of medical or vocational experts whose advice was obtained on behalf of the plan in connection with a claimant's adverse benefit determination, without regard to whether the advice was relied upon
rules.applies_to: ERISA group health plans; insurers and non-federal governmental plans through 2719 and 45 CFR 147.136.
rules.requires: Appeals get no deference to the first decision and are decided by a named fiduciary who did not make the first decision and is not that person's subordinate. Appeals involving medical judgment (medical necessity, experimental, appropriateness) require consulting a licensed health care professional ((m)(7): 'a physician or other health care professional licensed, accredited, or certified') with training in the relevant field who was not consulted on the first decision, and the plan must identify any experts consulted. Hiring, pay and promotion of adjudicators and medical experts may not depend on denials.
rules.deadline: Within the appeal decision deadline (E06).
rules.consequence: Failure is a procedural violation leading to deemed exhaustion (E09).
rules.provider_use: This is the lawful 'AI versus AI' lever: for any medical-judgment denial (medical necessity, Mohs appropriateness, modifier necessity), demand the name and specialty of the licensed professional consulted on appeal and confirmation the reviewer is independent of the first decision. An automated tool is not a 'health care professional' as defined in (m)(7).

rules.quote: In the case of a plan or issuer that fails to strictly adhere to all the requirements of this paragraph (b)(2) with respect to a claim, the claimant is deemed to have exhausted the internal claims and appeals process ... If a claimant chooses to pursue remedies under section 502(a) of ERISA under such circumstances, the claim or appeal is deemed denied on review without the exercise of discretion by an appropriate fiduciary. ... This exception is not available if the violation is part of a pattern or practice of violations by the plan or issuer. The claimant may request a written explanation of the violation from the plan or issuer, and the plan or issuer must provide such explanation within 10 days
rules.applies_to: Non-grandfathered group health plans (self-funded and insured) and issuers; non-federal governmental plans. For grandfathered and retiree-only plans the older 2560.503-1(l)(1) rule applies (deemed exhaustion for failure to follow procedures, without the 'strictly adhere' and 'without discretion' language).
rules.requires: Strict compliance with every 2560.503-1 and 2719(b)(2) requirement. Only a de minimis, non-prejudicial, good-cause violation in an ongoing good-faith exchange is excused, and never one that is part of a pattern or practice. On request the plan must explain in writing within 10 days why a violation should not count.
rules.deadline: Plan's written explanation of an alleged de minimis violation: 10 days from the claimant's request.
rules.consequence: The claimant may go straight to external review or to court; in an ERISA suit the claim is deemed denied without the exercise of discretion, which removes the deferential standard of review the plan otherwise relies on. This is the main legal leverage against a self-funded plan.
rules.provider_use: Every escalation letter should: (1) name each requirement violated with its subsection; (2) state that the internal process is deemed exhausted under 2719(b)(2)(ii)(F)(1); (3) request the 10-day written explanation under (F)(2); (4) state the concrete next step the practice will actually take (external review with patient authorization, or a 502(a)(1)(B) claim as assignee). RemitWatch can document repeat violations by the same plan, which defeats the de minimis exception ('pattern or practice').

rules.quote: A plan and issuer must allow a claimant to review the claim file and to present evidence and testimony as part of the internal claims and appeals process ... Before the plan or issuer can issue a final internal adverse benefit determination based on a new or additional rationale, the claimant must be provided, free of charge, with the rationale
rules.applies_to: Non-grandfathered group health plans and issuers; non-federal governmental plans.
rules.requires: Any new evidence considered or generated, and any new rationale, must be sent free and early enough for the claimant to respond before the final decision deadline (the deadline is tolled if it arrives too late).
rules.deadline: Before the appeal decision deadline, with a reasonable opportunity to respond.
rules.consequence: A final denial on a new reason without advance disclosure is a violation leading to deemed exhaustion.
rules.provider_use: When an appeal denial switches reasons (for example from 'not medically necessary' to 'bundled'), cite (C)(2), demand reopening, and treat the claim as deemed exhausted if refused.

rules.citation: 29 CFR 2560.503-1(b)(4); 29 CFR 2590.715-2719(a)(2)(iii); DOL Benefit Claims Procedure FAQs A-8 and B-2
rules.quote: (b)(4): "The claims procedures do not preclude an authorized representative of a claimant from acting on behalf of such claimant in pursuing a benefit claim or appeal of an adverse benefit determination." FAQ B-2: "Typically, assignments are not a grant of authority to act on a claimant's behalf in pursuing and appealing a benefit determination under a plan." FAQ A-8: "where a claimant may request payments for medical services from a plan but the medical provider will continue to have recourse against the claimant for amounts unpaid by the plan, the request, whether made by the claimant or by the medical provider (e.g., in the case of an assignment of benefits by the claimant) would constitute a claim for benefits by the claimant."
rules.applies_to: All ERISA plans. Where the practice is in-network and cannot bill the patient beyond cost sharing, DOL FAQ A-8 treats a pure payment dispute as a matter of the provider contract, not a benefit claim.
rules.requires: Plans must allow an authorized representative but may set reasonable procedures to verify the authorization. An assignment of benefits alone usually does not make the provider an authorized representative.
rules.deadline: None of its own.
rules.consequence: Without a proper designation the plan can treat the practice's appeal as not filed by the claimant; without a valid assignment the practice cannot sue (E12).
rules.provider_use: At intake collect both: (1) an assignment of the right to payment and of the right to pursue claims, appeals, external review and suit; and (2) a separate designation of authorized representative on the plan's own form when it has one. UHC's provider site says: 'An assignment of benefits does not constitute designation of an authorized representative.' For in-network rate disputes cite the provider agreement, not ERISA.

rules.citation: 29 U.S.C. 1132(a)(1)(B); Brown v. BlueCross BlueShield of Tenn., Inc., No. 15-5739 (6th Cir. June 27, 2016) (published, File Name 16a0147p.06; reported at 827 F.3d 543 per secondary sources)
rules.quote: We agree that the assignment of the right to payment is sufficient to confer derivative standing to bring suit for non-payment under ERISA. ... A healthcare provider-assignee "stands in the shoes of the beneficiary," and can only assert claims that could have been brought by patients themselves.
rules.applies_to: Federal courts in Kentucky (Sixth Circuit). Indiana is in the Seventh Circuit; Brown cites Kennedy v. Conn. Gen. Life Ins. Co., 924 F.2d 698, 701 (7th Cir. 1991) for provider-assignee standing (Kennedy itself not read).
rules.requires: Nothing of the payer directly; defines when the practice can sue: with a valid assignment, for benefits the patient could have claimed.
rules.deadline: Suit timing is governed by the plan's limitations clause if reasonable (Heimeshoff v. Hartford Life & Accident Ins. Co., No. 12-729 (U.S. Dec. 16, 2013): 'We hold that the Plan's limitations provision is enforceable.').
rules.consequence: Assignee can sue under 502(a)(1)(B) for unpaid benefits (coverage, denials). Disputes over the contract rate and recoupments under a provider agreement fall outside the assignment and are contract claims (Brown, Part IV).
rules.provider_use: Letters to self-funded plans may truthfully state that the practice holds the patient's assignment and has standing to recover benefits due under ERISA 502(a)(1)(B), for denials and non-payment. Do not frame in-network rate shortfalls as ERISA claims; frame them under the provider agreement.

rules.citation: Dialysis Newco, Inc. v. Community Health Systems Group Health Plan, No. 18-40863 (5th Cir. Sept. 11, 2019); Angelina Emergency Medicine Assocs. PA v. Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Ala., No. 24-10306 (5th Cir. opinion filed Aug. 8, 2025), cert. denied, No. 25-1020 (U.S. June 1, 2026)
rules.quote: Dialysis Newco: "when an ERISA plan contains a valid anti-assignment provision, a putative assignment to a healthcare provider is invalid and cannot bestow the provider with standing to sue under the plan." Angelina (quoting Hermann): "[i]t was MEBA's responsibility to notify Hermann of that clause if it intended to rely on it to avoid any attempted assignments."
rules.applies_to: Fifth Circuit law; persuasive only in Kentucky (6th Cir.) and Indiana (7th Cir.). Whether the 6th or 7th Circuit has a binding published holding on enforceability or waiver of health-plan anti-assignment clauses was not confirmed.
rules.requires: Nothing of the payer; explains the main defense to provider suits and how it is lost.
rules.deadline: None.
rules.consequence: A clear anti-assignment clause can defeat the practice's standing. A plan that pays in part, works the appeals and withholds the plan documents without ever raising the clause may be estopped from raising it later (Angelina, remanded for fact-finding). Dialysis Newco also held a Tennessee statute forcing plans to honor assignments preempted by ERISA.
rules.provider_use: In the first letter to each self-funded plan: state that the practice relies on the patient's assignment, ask the plan to identify in writing any anti-assignment provision it contends applies, and request the plan documents. Keep the authorized-representative designation (E11) as a fallback, because an anti-assignment clause does not bar an authorized representative.

rules.quote: 1144(b)(2)(B): "Neither an employee benefit plan ... nor any trust established under such a plan, shall be deemed to be an insurance company or other insurer ... for purposes of any law of any State purporting to regulate insurance companies, insurance contracts". KRS 304.17A-005(29): "'Insurer' means any insurance company; health maintenance organization; self-insurer, including a governmental plan, church plan, or multiple employer welfare arrangement, not exempt from state regulation by ERISA".
rules.applies_to: Self-funded private-employer ERISA plans and multiemployer plans: state insurance prompt-pay laws do not apply (deemer clause; and Kentucky's own definition covers only self-insurers not exempt by ERISA). Fully insured plans: state insurance law is saved (1144(b)(2)(A)). In Kentucky, self-insured governmental plans and church plans are 'insurers' by definition, so KRS 304.17A-700 to -730 reach them (ERISA does not apply to them).
rules.requires: Classify funding before choosing remedies. Kentucky also adopts the ERISA definition of adverse benefit determination for its insured-plan appeal statutes (KRS 304.17A-600(1)(a)).
rules.deadline: State prompt-pay deadlines apply only to insured, Kentucky governmental and church self-insured plans (details in the state-law area).
rules.consequence: No state prompt-pay interest or Department of Insurance enforcement against a self-funded private ERISA plan; the leverage there is federal (E02-E10, E18).
rules.provider_use: Never cite KRS 304.17A or Indiana prompt-pay to a self-funded private ERISA plan; it signals a weak letter. Do cite them to fully insured plans and to Kentucky public-employer and church self-insured plans. Determine funding from the ID card, the 835 (self-funded or ASO notes), the employer's Form 5500 (E21), or by asking the payer.

rules.citation: Laurel Hill Mgmt. Servs., Inc. v. La-Z-Boy Inc., No. 25-1727 (6th Cir. Aug. 19, 2026)
rules.quote: (as reported by Mayer Brown) ERISA preempts the providers' claims "when those claims arise out of an ERISA-plan administrator's oral assurances" "about the coverage or reimbursement under an ERISA-governed plan."
rules.applies_to: Kentucky (Sixth Circuit); out-of-network providers suing on verification-call representations about an ERISA plan's terms. Other circuits are split.
rules.requires: Nothing of the payer.
rules.deadline: None.
rules.consequence: State-law negligent misrepresentation and promissory estoppel claims based on benefits verification calls are preempted in the Sixth Circuit.
rules.provider_use: In Kentucky, do not threaten state-law misrepresentation suits against self-funded plans over verification calls; rely on ERISA remedies. Full opinion text was not read (paywalled); confirm before relying on details.

rules.citation: 29 U.S.C. 1024(b)(4); 29 U.S.C. 1132(c)(1); 29 CFR 2575.502c-1; 29 U.S.C. 1002(16)(A); DOL Benefit Claims Procedure FAQ C-17
rules.quote: 1024(b)(4): "The administrator shall, upon written request of any participant or beneficiary, furnish a copy of the latest updated summary, plan description, and the latest annual report, any terminal report, the bargaining agreement, trust agreement, contract, or other instruments under which the plan is established or operated." 1132(c)(1): "by mailing the material requested to the last known address of the requesting participant or beneficiary within 30 days after such request may in the court's discretion be personally liable to such participant or beneficiary in the amount of up to $100 a day". 2575.502c-1: "increased from $100 a day to $110 a day".
rules.applies_to: ERISA plans. The duty and penalty run against the plan 'administrator' (the person designated in the plan, otherwise the plan sponsor, usually the employer or the multiemployer board), not the claims TPA, and only for requests by a participant or beneficiary.
rules.requires: Plan documents, SPD, and other instruments (DOL says internal rules and criteria count, FAQ C-17) within 30 days of a written request by a participant or beneficiary; reasonable copy charge allowed.
rules.deadline: 30 days from the participant's written request.
rules.consequence: Up to $110 per day, in the court's discretion, payable to the participant or beneficiary.
rules.provider_use: Run the request through the patient: the patient (or the practice as the patient's designated authorized representative) sends a written request to the plan administrator named in the SPD or Form 5500. Whether a provider-assignee can recover 502(c) penalties in the 6th or 7th Circuit was not confirmed, so letters should not claim the penalty as the practice's own right.

rules.quote: the court in its discretion may allow a reasonable attorney's fee and costs of action to either party.
rules.applies_to: Actions under ERISA Title I by a participant, beneficiary or fiduciary (an assignee sues in the patient's shoes).
rules.requires: Nothing of the payer until a court rules.
rules.deadline: None.
rules.consequence: Fee-shifting is possible in either direction, at the court's discretion.
rules.provider_use: A truthful line: an ERISA suit for benefits can carry an award of attorney's fees. Do not imply fees are automatic. Small claims only make sense in court when aggregated per plan.

rules.quote: There is hereby imposed a tax on any failure of a group health plan to meet the requirements of chapter 100 (relating to group health plan requirements). ... The amount of the tax imposed by subsection (a) on any failure shall be $100 for each day in the noncompliance period with respect to each individual to whom such failure relates.
rules.applies_to: Group health plans under IRC chapter 100, which by 26 U.S.C. 9815(a)(1) includes PHSA part A (and so the 2719 claims and appeals rules) and the No Surprises Act sections 9816-9817: private-employer self-funded and insured plans (the employer is liable), multiemployer plans (the plan is liable), church plans. Not governmental plans (9831(a)(1)); not plans with fewer than 2 current-employee participants (9831(a)(2)); insured small employers (2-50 employees) are exempt for failures caused solely by the insurer's coverage (4980D(d)).
rules.requires: Plan sponsor must self-report and pay on Form 8928 (26 CFR 54.6011-2).
rules.deadline: No tax if the failure was due to reasonable cause and is corrected within 30 days after the person knew or should have known (4980D(c)(2)).
rules.consequence: $100 per day per affected individual; caps for unintentional failures (lesser of 10% of prior-year group health plan spend or $500,000).
rules.provider_use: Addressed to the plan administrator or sponsor, a letter can state accurately that the claims and appeals rules of PHSA 2719 are part of IRC chapter 100 (26 U.S.C. 9815) and that uncorrected failures carry a self-reported excise tax under 26 U.S.C. 4980D. Notice from the practice also starts the 30-day correction window. There is no verified channel for a provider to 'report' the tax, so do not threaten an IRS report. That claims-procedure failures are 4980D 'failures' follows from the statutory text; IRS enforcement practice was not confirmed.

rules.quote: The maximum amount of penalty imposed under this paragraph is $100 for each day for each individual with respect to which such a failure occurs. (45 CFR 102.3 lists the 2025 maximum adjusted penalty for 300gg-22(b)(2)(C)(i) as $188.)
rules.applies_to: Non-federal governmental group health plans (state, county, city, public school and university self-funded plans) and health insurance issuers where HHS enforces. Self-funded governmental plans cannot opt out of the 2719 claims and appeals rules (2719 is not on the 146.180(a)(1) opt-out list).
rules.requires: Compliance with 45 CFR 147.136 (same internal claims, appeals and external review rules as ERISA plans).
rules.deadline: No penalty if corrected within 30 days of knowledge and due to reasonable cause.
rules.consequence: HHS (CMS) civil money penalty up to $188 per day per affected individual (2025 adjusted figure).
rules.provider_use: For Kentucky and Indiana public-employer plans, cite 45 CFR 147.136 and CMS's enforcement authority; complaints go to CMS. In Kentucky these plans are also subject to the state prompt-pay statute (E14).

rules.quote: A group health plan or health insurance issuer must allow a claimant to file a request for an external review with the plan or issuer if the request is filed within four months after the date of receipt of a notice of an adverse benefit determination or final internal adverse benefit determination. ... Upon receipt of a notice of a final external review decision reversing the adverse benefit determination or final adverse benefit determination, the plan or issuer immediately must provide coverage or payment (including immediately authorizing care or immediately paying benefits) for the claim.
rules.applies_to: Non-grandfathered self-funded ERISA plans (federal process; must contract with at least 3 IROs and rotate); insured plans use the state process if it meets NAIC standards (Kentucky and Indiana processes are in the state-law area). Scope: denials involving medical judgment (medical necessity, appropriateness, setting, level of care, effectiveness, experimental), No Surprises Act compliance, and rescissions; eligibility denials are excluded. Pure contract-rate or coding-policy disputes without medical judgment are likely outside scope.
rules.requires: Plan: preliminary review within 5 business days and written notice within 1 business day; assign an accredited IRO; send the file within 5 business days of assignment; no cost to the claimant. IRO: de novo review; decision within 45 days. Reversal: plan pays immediately.
rules.deadline: Request within 4 months of the notice; 5 business days preliminary review; 5 business days to send file to IRO; 45 days IRO decision; immediate payment after reversal. Expedited: 72 hours.
rules.consequence: Decision binds the plan (except other remedies). If the plan does not send the file on time, 'the assigned IRO may terminate the external review and make a decision to reverse'.
rules.provider_use: Usable for medical-necessity, Mohs appropriateness and similar medical-judgment denials, with the patient's authorization (the claimant includes an authorized representative; Cigna's page says 'the health care provider must get their patient's approval to proceed'). Deemed exhaustion (E09) lets the practice skip remaining internal appeals and go straight here. Batch requests per plan; each claim is decided separately.

rules.quote: Q42 (tool-extracted): "The EFAST2 website publicly shows successfully submitted Form 5500, 5500-SF, and PR filings". 29 CFR 2520.104-20(a): the administrator of a welfare plan covering "fewer than 100 participants" that meets (b) "is not required to file with the Secretary an annual or terminal report."
rules.applies_to: ERISA welfare plans that file Form 5500 (generally 100 or more participants, or funded trusts such as multiemployer funds). Small unfunded or insured plans do not file.
rules.requires: Public disclosure of the plan name, plan number, sponsor, EIN and administrator for filing plans.
rules.deadline: None.
rules.consequence: Not a remedy; a targeting tool.
rules.provider_use: Look up each self-funded employer group once and store the plan administrator's legal name and address, so escalation letters reach the party legally responsible for the claims procedure and the excise tax rather than only the TPA. Batchable across all employer groups.

rules.quote: A covered entity may use or disclose protected health information for its own treatment, payment, or health care operations. ... Payment means: (1) The activities undertaken by: ... (ii) A health care provider or health plan to obtain or provide reimbursement for the provision of health care ... a covered entity or business associate must make reasonable efforts to limit protected health information to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose
rules.applies_to: The practice (a HIPAA covered entity) when it escalates to a plan sponsor or employer.
rules.requires: Disclosures to obtain payment are permitted but limited to the minimum necessary.
rules.deadline: None.
rules.consequence: An over-broad disclosure to an employer's HR or benefits office is a HIPAA risk for the practice.
rules.provider_use: When copying the plan administrator or sponsor, list claim numbers, dates of service and amounts only; keep diagnoses and clinical records for the plan's appeals unit.

rules.quote: The Combined Fund shall be— (A) a plan described in section 302(c)(5) of the Labor Management Relations Act, 1947 (29 U.S.C. 186(c)(5)), (B) an employee welfare benefit plan within the meaning of section 3(1) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (29 U.S.C. 1002(1)), and (C) a multiemployer plan within the meaning of section 3(37) of such Act (29 U.S.C. 1002(37)).
rules.applies_to: UMWA Combined Benefit Fund and 1992 UMWA Benefit Plan (statutory text; 9712(a)(2) is identical in substance). The 1993 Benefit Plan was not checked. Because they are 302(c)(5) jointly trusteed plans, the collective-bargaining deeming rule in 2560.503-1(b)(6) does not apply, so the full claims regulation applies; the quarterly-board timing rule in (i)(2)(iii)(B) may apply to appeals. The ACA 2719 rules do not apply to any plan year in which a plan has fewer than 2 participants who are current employees (29 U.S.C. 1191a(a)); whether the UMWA plans are retiree-only was not confirmed.
rules.requires: Non-Medicare members: ERISA claims and appeal rules (E02-E09). UMWA's own page for non-Medicare members: appeal 'within 180 days of receipt of your Explanation of Benefits (EOB)'; decision 'not later than 30 days after receipt of your request for review'; second level decided within 30 days post-service; civil action under ERISA 502(a) after a final adverse decision. Provider billing FAQ: 'The timely filing is 12 months from the date of service for claims'; 'An appeal of a denied claim must be filed within 180 days of the date of denial.'
rules.deadline: Timely filing 12 months from date of service; provider appeal of a denied claim within 180 days of denial; Funds decision 30 days per level (non-Medicare).
rules.consequence: Same ERISA consequences as any plan (deemed exhaustion, 502(a) suit).
rules.provider_use: Provider appeals and disputes: UMWA Health & Retirement Funds, P.O. Box 211225, Eagan, MN 55121-2625 (billing FAQ). Non-Medicare member appeals: Attention: Appeals Department, PO Box 292167, Nashville, TN 37229. No appeal fax number was found.

rules.quote: 417.840: "The HCPP must apply § 422.568 through § 422.626 of this chapter to— (a) Organization determinations and fast-track appeals that affect its Medicare enrollees". 417.832(b): "Physicians and other individuals who furnish items or services under arrangements with an HCPP have no right of administrative review under §§ 417.834 through 417.840." 422.568(c): "The MA organization must process requests for payment according to the 'prompt payment' provisions set forth in § 422.520."
rules.applies_to: UMWA Funds members who are Medicare enrollees. UMWA's site: 'The Funds is a Medicare Health Care Prepayment Plan (HCPP) and is the Medicare payer for non-facility Part B services'; 'Providers must bill the Funds for Medicare Part B services.'; 'Medicare carriers will not pay for Part B services provided to Funds' beneficiaries.'
rules.requires: Medicare Advantage-style organization determinations and reconsiderations. A non-contract provider is a party if it waives the right to bill the enrollee (422.574(b)); UMWA's page: a non-plan doctor may appeal if the doctor 'completes a waiver of liability statement'. Reconsideration request within 60 calendar days after receipt of the notice (receipt presumed 5 days after the notice date). Payment reconsideration decided within 60 calendar days; if the Funds affirm or miss the deadline, the file goes to the CMS independent review entity (422.590(b)(2), (d)).
rules.deadline: Provider/enrollee: 60 calendar days to request reconsideration. Funds: 60 calendar days for payment reconsideration, then auto-forward to the IRE.
rules.consequence: A missed reconsideration deadline is an affirmation that goes to the CMS IRE (422.590(d)); failure to give timely notice of an organization determination is itself an adverse determination that may be appealed (422.568(f)). Whether 422.520's 30-day clean-claim payment and interest rule binds the HCPP through 422.568(c) is a textual argument not confirmed with CMS.
rules.provider_use: Route UMWA Medicare claims to the Medicare-style process, not the ERISA one. If the practice is a Funds 'Cooperating Provider' (under arrangement), 417.832(b) removes Medicare administrative review rights; use the Funds' provider dispute address instead. Whether the practice is a Cooperating Provider is unknown.

rules.citation: 29 CFR 2590.716-3 (definition of health care facility); 29 CFR 2590.716-5(b), (c)(3)-(4); 45 CFR 149.420(b)(1)(i); CMS/DOL/Treasury ACA-CAA FAQs Part 55, Q16-Q17 (Aug. 19, 2022)
rules.quote: Not later than 30 calendar days after the bill for the items or services is transmitted by the provider ... must determine whether the items and services are covered under the plan or coverage and, if the items and services are covered, send to the provider an initial payment or a notice of denial of payment. For purposes of this paragraph (c)(3), the 30-calendar-day period begins on the date the plan or issuer receives the information necessary to decide a claim for payment for the items or services.
rules.applies_to: Only out-of-network (nonparticipating) services at an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department, critical access hospital or ambulatory surgical center, or emergency services; all private group health plans (self-funded and insured) and issuers, including grandfathered plans. Not the practice's own office (not a 'health care facility' for non-emergency services). Pathology and radiology are 'ancillary services' for which the notice-and-consent waiver is never available (45 CFR 149.420(b)(1)(i)).
rules.requires: Initial payment or denial within 30 calendar days of a clean bill, paid directly to the provider; cost sharing at in-network levels; total payment equal to the out-of-network rate less cost sharing.
rules.deadline: 30 calendar days from receipt of a clean claim.
rules.consequence: The provider's 30-business-day open-negotiation window does not start until the initial payment or denial is sent (FAQ Part 55 Q17). Complaints: No Surprises Help Desk 1-800-985-3059 or https://www.cms.gov/nosurprises/policies-and-resources/providers-submit-a-billing-complaint. Plans also face 4980D (E18).
rules.provider_use: Flag claims where the practice was out-of-network with the plan and the service was furnished at an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ASC (for example pathology read for such a facility). For those only: cite 716-5(c)(3), use the CMS complaint channel for late payment, and consider open negotiation and IDR (E26).

rules.quote: 716-6(d)(1)(ii): "If the qualifying payment amount is based on a downcoded service code or modifier— (A) A statement that the service code or modifier billed by the provider ... was downcoded; (B) An explanation of why the claim was downcoded". 149.510(b)(1)(i): "during the 30-business-day period beginning on the day the provider ... receives an initial payment or notice of denial of payment regarding the item or service, initiate a 30-business-day open negotiation period". (b)(2)(i): "during the 4-business-day period beginning on the first business day after the last day of the open negotiation period". (c)(5)(ix): "must be paid directly to the provider ... not later than 30 calendar days after the determination by the certified IDR entity."
rules.applies_to: Only No Surprises Act claims (E25).
rules.requires: With each initial payment or denial: the QPA, a certification it was calculated correctly, and, if downcoded, a statement and explanation of the downcoding and the QPA without downcoding. Open negotiation, then IDR; IDR payment within 30 calendar days of the decision. A certified IDR entity may decide up to 50 qualifying items in one batched dispute if (c)(4)(i) conditions are met.
rules.deadline: Open negotiation: start within 30 business days after receiving the initial payment or denial; negotiation lasts 30 business days. IDR: initiate within 4 business days after it ends. IDR payment: 30 calendar days after the determination.
rules.consequence: IDR determinations are binding; the losing party keeps the IDR entity fee (fee ranges $200-$840 single and $268-$1,173 batched plus $75-$250 per extra 25 lines, (e)(2)(viii)); administrative fee $15 per party per dispute for disputes initiated on or after June 11, 2026 ((d)(2)(ii)(B)).
rules.provider_use: Relevant to RemitWatch's downcoding detection only for NSA-covered out-of-network claims: the plan must disclose and explain downcoding with the initial payment. Note the 2026 IDR operations rule (91 FR 34070, June 4, 2026; 91 FR 55468, Aug. 28, 2026) applies parts of (b) and (c)(4) only to open negotiation periods beginning 90 days after the Departments announce the system is ready; until then the prior text governs (timing not compared line by line).

rules.quote: A group health plan or health insurance issuer must make available on an internet website the information required under paragraph (b)(1) of this section in three machine-readable files ... An in-network rate machine-readable file that includes the required information under this paragraph (b)(1)(i) for all covered items and services
rules.applies_to: Non-grandfathered group health plans (self-funded plans usually through their TPA by written agreement, which leaves the plan liable if the TPA fails) and group issuers.
rules.requires: Public in-network rate file listing negotiated rates by billing code for each coverage option and provider.
rules.deadline: Files must be updated monthly and show the last update date ((b)(3)).
rules.consequence: Not a provider remedy by itself; it is the plan's own published statement of the contract rate.
rules.provider_use: For in-network underpayments against the contract rate, cite the plan's own posted negotiated rate for the practice's TIN or NPI and the CPT code as evidence in the provider-agreement dispute. An amendment published at 91 FR 63859 (Oct. 6, 2026) was not reviewed.

rules.citation: UMR provider FAQ UM1491 (2024); Cigna appeals and disputes page; UnitedHealthcare provider appeals page
rules.quote: UMR: "UMR is an affiliate of UnitedHealthcare and is not an insurance company. UMR is a third-party administrator (TPA)"; "Timely filing limits can vary based on the provider's contract and/or the self-funded benefit plan."; "The customer chooses which day of the week/month to release payment." Cigna (tool-extracted): "Submit the appeal within 180 calendar days of the date of the initial payment"; "you must request arbitration within one year of the date of the letter". UHC (tool-extracted): "An assignment of benefits does not constitute designation of an authorized representative."
rules.applies_to: UMR self-funded customers and UHC Shared Services (same claim address); Cigna insured and administrative-services plans; UnitedHealthcare commercial.
rules.requires: UMR: appeals online at umr.com or to UMR-Claim Appeals, PO Box 30546, Salt Lake City, UT 84130; check tracer 30 days after the check issue date. Cigna: provider appeal within 180 calendar days of the initial payment or denial (or last adjustment); review completed in 60 days; arbitration for contracted disputes within one year of the final internal decision. UHC: two-step reconsideration then appeal; commercial timelines per participation agreement.
rules.deadline: Cigna 180 calendar days; UMR and UHC per plan and contract (not stated as a single number).
rules.consequence: Contract and manual limits can be shorter than ERISA's 180-day member appeal window for contract disputes; for benefit claims the ERISA minimums apply to the plan.
rules.provider_use: File through the channel each payer names (no UMR appeal fax was listed). UMR claims can be 'processed' but not funded until the employer releases payment; a check tracer is available at 30 days.

batch_and_channel: Clocks start only when a claim or appeal is filed under the plan's reasonable procedures (2560.503-1(f)(4), (i)(4)). Send appeals and record requests to the exact appeal address, portal or fax the plan names; a fax to a general number can be treated as not filed. Keep transmission proof as the receipt date.

UMR (and UHC Shared Services): appeals online at umr.com or by mail to UMR-Claim Appeals, PO Box 30546, Salt Lake City, UT 84130; its provider FAQ lists no appeal fax; UMR has its own post-service appeal request form, so use it to avoid a 'not filed' argument.

UMWA Funds: provider appeals and disputes by mail to P.O. Box 211225, Eagan, MN 55121-2625 (claims go to P.O. Box 211551); non-Medicare member appeals to Appeals Department, PO Box 292167, Nashville, TN 37229; Medicare members follow the HCPP reconsideration process (60 days). No appeal fax number was found.

Batch by payer and by violation, not by claim: one letter can list many claims for the same plan with the same defect (no determination by day 30, missing plan provision, missing standard, missing criteria) and request the claim files and criteria for all of them. The regulation sets no per-claim form; follow any form the plan requires.
Use RemitWatch's history to prove a 'pattern or practice' of violations per plan; that removes the plan's only excuse for a procedural violation (2719(b)(2)(ii)(F)(2)).

Deadlines to automate: claim decision day 30 (day 45 with a timely extension notice); practice appeal 180 days from receipt of the notice (check SPD and contract); plan appeal decision 60 days (one level) or 30 days per level; plan's written explanation of an alleged minor violation 10 days; external review request 4 months; plan preliminary review 5 business days; IRO decision 45 days; Cigna provider appeal 180 calendar days; UMWA timely filing 12 months and appeal 180 days of denial; UMWA Medicare reconsideration 60 days.

No Surprises Act claims only: 30 calendar days to initial payment; 30 business days to start open negotiation; 4 business days to start IDR; up to 50 qualifying items per batched IDR dispute under 45 CFR 149.510(c)(4)(i); $15 administrative fee per party (disputes on or after June 11, 2026); IDR payment within 30 calendar days of the decision.

Escalation ladder for self-funded plans: (1) appeals unit with the compliance list; (2) deemed-exhaustion notice with the 10-day explanation request; (3) copy to the plan administrator named in the SPD or Form 5500 (EFAST2), minimum necessary information only; (4) external review with patient authorization for medical-judgment denials; (5) patient-filed request for plan documents and EBSA help ((866) 444-3272; EBSA Benefits Advisors recovered $468.7 million in FY 2025 through informal resolution); (6) aggregated 502(a)(1)(B) suit as assignee.

For low-dollar balances, the cheapest lawful pressure is the batched per-plan compliance demand plus deemed-exhaustion notice; per-claim external review needs patient authorization and is worth it mainly for repeat denial patterns or large claims.
does_not_apply: Kentucky prompt-pay (KRS 304.17A-700 to -730) does not apply to self-funded private-employer ERISA plans or multiemployer plans: ERISA's deemer clause (29 U.S.C. 1144(b)(2)(B)) and Kentucky's own definition of insurer, which covers only self-insurers 'not exempt from state regulation by ERISA' (KRS 304.17A-005(29), 304.17A-700(12)). The Indiana statute was not read here; the same deemer clause applies.

ERISA has no prompt-pay interest or late-payment penalty for non-No Surprises Act claims; the claims rules set decision deadlines, not payment deadlines. Prejudgment interest in an ERISA suit is at the court's discretion (standard not confirmed).

The ERISA 502(c)(1) penalty (up to $110 per day) runs only against the plan 'administrator' (usually the employer or the board, not UMR, Cigna or UHC as claims administrator) and only for requests by a participant or beneficiary; a provider-assignee's right to it was not confirmed.

The 2719 additions (strict-adherence deemed exhaustion, notice extras, federal external review) do not apply to grandfathered plans (except for No Surprises Act external review) or to plans with fewer than two current-employee participants (retiree-only plans, 29 U.S.C. 1191a(a)); the base 2560.503-1 rules still apply to those ERISA plans.

Federal external review does not cover eligibility denials, and pure contract-rate or coding-policy disputes with no medical judgment are likely outside its scope (2719(d)(1)(i)(A)). It is the patient's process, so it needs the patient's authorization.

For in-network services where the practice cannot bill the patient beyond cost sharing, a payment-rate dispute is generally a provider-contract matter, not an ERISA benefit claim (DOL FAQ A-8); rate and recoupment disputes fall outside the patient's assignment (Brown v. BCBST). Use the provider agreement's dispute and arbitration terms.

The No Surprises Act plan rules do not reach services in the practice's own office (not a hospital, hospital outpatient department, critical access hospital or ASC) or in-network claims; they bind group health plans and health insurance issuers (29 CFR 2590.716-5(a)). Medicare, Medicaid, VA and TRICARE have their own balance-billing rules, not reviewed here.

In the Sixth Circuit, provider state-law negligent misrepresentation and promissory estoppel claims based on verification calls about an ERISA plan's terms are preempted (Laurel Hill v. La-Z-Boy, Aug. 19, 2026, secondary source).
State laws that force plans to honor assignments do not override an ERISA plan's anti-assignment clause (Dialysis Newco, 5th Cir. 2019, Tennessee statute preempted).

The 4980D excise tax is self-reported by the employer or multiemployer plan on Form 8928; a provider cannot file it, and it does not apply to governmental plans or to small insured employers' failures caused solely by the insurer.

UMWA Medicare members' Part B claims are not ERISA appeals: they follow 42 CFR 417.840 and 422.568-422.626; physicians furnishing services 'under arrangements with an HCPP' have no Medicare administrative review rights (417.832(b)).

Medigap (Medicare supplement) policies and Medicare crossover rules were not researched in this area; employer retiree plans that pay secondary to Medicare are ERISA plans and follow the claims rules above.
open_questions: Whether the Sixth Circuit (Kentucky) or Seventh Circuit (Indiana) has a binding published decision enforcing, or finding waiver of, an anti-assignment clause in an ERISA health plan was not confirmed.
Whether a provider-assignee can recover ERISA 502(c)(1) document penalties in the Sixth or Seventh Circuit was not confirmed.
Prejudgment interest standard and rate for ERISA benefit awards in the Sixth and Seventh Circuits was not researched.

Whether the UMWA 1992 Plan, 1993 Plan and Combined Fund have fewer than two current-employee participants (retiree-only exemption from 2719) was not confirmed; whether the practice is a UMWA Cooperating Provider (which removes Medicare administrative review rights under 417.832(b)) is unknown.
Whether the 42 CFR 422.520 clean-claim payment and interest rule binds the UMWA HCPP through 422.568(c) as incorporated by 417.840 is a textual argument only; not confirmed with CMS.
Kentucky Employees' Health Plan funding status was not confirmed; if self-insured governmental, Kentucky prompt-pay applies by definition (KRS 304.17A-005(29)).
Indiana Code (IC 27-8-5.7 and any TPA provisions) was not read because iga.in.gov did not serve text; left to the state-law area.

Anthem Kentucky and Indiana commercial and administrative-services dispute timelines, and UHC commercial reconsideration and appeal day limits, depend on the practice's participation agreements and current manuals; not confirmed.
Laurel Hill v. La-Z-Boy full opinion not read (paywalled); relied on law-firm summaries.
Angelina: the Supreme Court docket lists the Fifth Circuit decision date as Oct. 23, 2025, while the opinion read is dated Aug. 8, 2025; a revised opinion may exist.
The Transparency in Coverage amendment at 91 FR 63859 (Oct. 6, 2026) was not reviewed.
Whether the Departments have issued the guidance that triggers the 2026 IDR operations rule's new open-negotiation and batching procedures (45 CFR 149.510(h)) was not checked.
Whether EBSA accepts complaints filed by providers (as opposed to participants) was not confirmed; its page addresses workers and employers.
Whether courts treat an 835 remittance sent to the provider-assignee as the required adverse benefit determination notice (rather than the member EOB) was not researched.
DOL FAQ, Cigna, UHC and UMWA page quotes were extracted with a fetch tool because those sites blocked direct download; spot-check the exact wording before quoting them in letters.
